posts.title: How to get your first Fiverr order: a system, not luck
posts.seo_title: How to get your first Fiverr order: a system, not luck | Freelancer College
posts.description: Bevin waited almost a year for his first Fiverr order. This is the system that ended the silence, step by step.
posts.cover: Your first order is a system.
posts.body:
Almost a year. That is how long Bevin waited for his first Fiverr order. Not because he lacked skill, but because he had no system. Here is what changed.

1. Stop selling everything

A gig that says "I will do any design" competes with millions of others. A gig that says "I will design a mobile app UI for fitness startups" competes with a handful. Specific wins.

2. Match your portfolio to your gig

If your gig sells app UI, your gig images and portfolio must show app UI. Three strong, relevant samples beat twenty random ones. Buyers decide in seconds.

3. Write the title for search, the description for humans

Your title should contain the words buyers type: "mobile app UI", "Figma", "landing page". Your description should talk about the buyer's problem first, then how you solve it. Our free AI gig generator gives you a strong first draft.

4. Price with three packages

Basic to get clicks, Standard as the real offer, Premium to make Standard look reasonable. Read the biggest pricing mistake before you set yours.

5. Be active and fast

  • Reply to messages within an hour when you can. Response time matters.
  • Stay online during your buyers' working hours, not just yours.
  • Send thoughtful Buyer Request replies, not copy paste templates.

6. Improve weekly, not randomly

Every week, check impressions, clicks and messages. Low impressions means fix the title and tags. Low clicks means fix the thumbnail and price. Low orders after messages means fix your replies.

The silence at the start is normal. Staying in it is optional.

Want to do this with guidance and feedback? That is exactly what Designer X is built for.

posts.title: The biggest pricing mistake Sri Lankan freelancers make
posts.seo_title: The biggest pricing mistake Sri Lankan freelancers make | Freelancer College
posts.description: Pricing for the local market when you sell to the world. Why it keeps you busy and broke, and how to price in dollars without losing orders.
posts.body:
You open Fiverr, look at what other sellers from Sri Lanka charge, and price yourself a little lower so you get noticed. It feels smart. It is the most expensive decision you will make as a freelancer.

The mistake: pricing for the wrong market

Your buyers are not in Colombo. They are in New York, London, Sydney and Berlin. A US startup founder does not compare your price to a Sri Lankan salary. They compare it to what a designer in their own country costs.

When you price at $5 for a logo or $15 for a landing page, you do not look affordable. You look risky. Serious buyers skip you, and the buyers who stay are the ones who want unlimited revisions for nothing.

Cheap prices do not attract good clients. They repel them.

What low prices actually cost you

  • More work for less money. You need ten small orders to earn what one proper order pays.
  • Worse clients. The lowest budgets usually come with the most demands.
  • No time to improve. You are too busy delivering cheap work to build the skills that get better work.
  • A ceiling on your reviews. Your profile fills with small jobs that do not prove you can handle big ones.

How to price on value instead

Start from the outcome the buyer gets, not the hours you spend. A landing page that brings in customers is worth far more to a business than the time it took you to design it.

  1. Pick a specific buyer. "SaaS startups" can pay more than "anyone who needs a website".
  2. Build three packages. Basic, Standard and Premium. Make Standard the obvious choice.
  3. Price Standard around a real hourly rate. Even as a beginner, aim for $12 to $15 an hour of real work.
  4. Raise prices after every five good reviews. Small steps, consistently.
Try it now: the free freelance price calculator turns your hours, skill and income goal into three USD packages.

"But I won't get orders if I charge more"

You will get fewer inquiries from the wrong people and more from the right ones. The fix for no orders is almost never a lower price. It is a clearer niche, a better portfolio and a gig that speaks to one type of buyer.

That is the whole idea behind LEAP: learn the skill, execute real projects, assemble a portfolio that gets chosen, then pitch and price like a professional. Never work for less.

posts.title: UI vs UX explained simply, and which one pays
posts.seo_title: UI vs UX explained simply (and which one pays) | Freelancer College
posts.description: The difference between UI and UX design in plain language, what each designer actually does, and why clients pay for both together.
posts.cover: UI is how it looks. UX is how it works.
posts.body:
UI and UX get mixed up all the time. Here is the simplest way to understand them, and why the freelancers who understand both earn the most.

UX: how it works

UX (user experience) is about the journey. Can people find what they need? Is checkout easy? Do they understand what to do next? UX designers research users, map flows and sketch wireframes before anything looks pretty.

UI: how it looks

UI (user interface) is the visual layer. Colors, typography, buttons, spacing and icons. UI designers make the structure beautiful, consistent and clear.

UXUI
QuestionDoes it work for people?Does it look and feel right?
OutputsResearch, flows, wireframesScreens, styles, components
ToolsInterviews, FigJam, FigmaFigma

Which one pays?

Clients rarely want only one. A startup wants an app that works and looks great. Freelancers who can do both, and explain their decisions, are the ones who win bigger projects and charge in dollars.

Start with the free 90 Day UI/UX Designer Path, or learn both live in Sinhala in Designer X.
